The cramped streets and courts eventually opened into a broad space, dotted with cattle pens and other signs of a livestock market. On reaching it Sikes slowed his steps, for the girl could no longer sustain the speed at which they had been walking. He turned to Oliver and harshly ordered him to take Nancy’s hand.

“Do you hear me?” Sikes snarled, as Oliver hesitated and glanced about him.

They stood in a gloomy corner, well away from passing travellers.

Oliver understood only too clearly that resistance was useless. He extended his hand, and Nancy gripped it firmly in her own.

“Give me the other one,” said Sikes, catching Oliver’s free hand. “Here, Bull’s-eye!”

The dog raised its head and growled.

“Look here, boy!” said Sikes, laying his other hand against Oliver’s throat. “If he so much as whispers, catch hold of him! Understand?”

The dog growled once more, licking its lips and watching Oliver as though eager to fasten upon his windpipe immediately.

“He’s as willing as any Christian, blind me if he ain’t!” said Sikes, surveying the creature with a grim, savage satisfaction. “Now you know what’s in store, young master. Shout as soon as you please; the dog’ll soon put a stop to that. Move along, youngster!”

Bull’s-eye wagged his tail in response to this unusually affectionate address and, after uttering another warning growl for Oliver’s benefit, trotted ahead.

They were crossing Smithfield, though for all Oliver knew it could equally have been Grosvenor Square. The night was foggy and dark. Shop lights scarcely pierced the dense mist, which grew thicker from moment to moment, wrapping houses and streets in shadow. To Oliver’s eyes it made this unfamiliar place stranger still, and deepened the misery and depression of his uncertainty.

They had hurried a few steps farther when a deep-toned church bell sounded the hour. At its first note both his guides halted and turned toward the sound.

“Eight o’clock, Bill,” Nancy said when the bell fell silent.

“What’s the use of telling me? I can hear it myself, can’t I?” Sikes answered.

“I wonder if they can hear it,” said Nancy.

“Of course they can,” returned Sikes. “It was Bartlemy fair when I got put away, and there wasn’t a penny trumpet there whose squeaking I couldn’t hear. Once they’d locked me in for the night, all that racket outside made the blasted old prison seem so silent I could near have dashed my brains against the door’s iron plates.”

To observe a star in passing glances—to regard it obliquely, presenting to it the outer regions of the retina, which are more responsive to faint light than the inner ones—is to see it clearly and perceive its radiance most fully. That radiance diminishes in exact proportion as we direct our sight squarely upon it. More rays indeed enter the eye in the latter instance, but in the former there is a subtler power of apprehension. Excessive depth confuses and weakens our thinking; even Venus herself may be made to disappear from the heavens by an inspection too prolonged, too concentrated, or too direct.

“As to these murders, let us undertake a few investigations of our own before forming a judgment. The inquiry will provide some amusement,” [I found the word oddly chosen in these circumstances, but remained silent] “and, moreover, Le Bon once did me a kindness that I have not forgotten. We shall visit the place and see it for ourselves. I am acquainted with G——, the Prefect of Police, and can readily secure the required permission.”

Permission was secured, and we set out immediately for the Rue Morgue. It is among the wretched streets lying between the Rue Richelieu and the Rue St. Roch. We arrived late in the afternoon, since the district was far removed from our own. The house was easy to locate: a number of people still stood across the street, staring with aimless curiosity at its shuttered windows. It was a commonplace Parisian dwelling, with a gateway beside which stood a glazed watch-box; a sliding pane in its window identified it as the concierge’s lodge. Before entering we continued along the street, turned into an alley, and turned once more to pass behind the building. All the while Dupin surveyed both the house and its surroundings with such minute attention that I could imagine no purpose for it.

We retraced our route to the front of the house, rang the bell, and, after presenting our authorization, were admitted by the officers in charge. Upstairs we entered the room where Mademoiselle L’Espanaye’s body had been discovered, and where both dead women still lay. The room’s confusion had been left untouched, as was customary. I noticed nothing beyond the particulars reported in the “Gazette des Tribunaux.” Dupin examined everything closely, including the victims’ bodies. Afterwards we inspected the remaining rooms and the yard, with a gendarme accompanying us the entire time.

Giving herself no leisure to reflect, and hardly aware of her own feelings, Elizabeth, as soon as she finished this letter, snatched up the other. She opened it with extreme impatience and read the following; it had been composed one day after the first was completed.

“By now, my dearest sister, my hasty letter must have reached you. I hope this one will be clearer, though, while I am not pressed for time, my thoughts are so confused that I cannot promise any coherence. Dearest Lizzy, I scarcely know what to say, but I must give you bad news without further delay. However imprudent a marriage between Mr. Wickham and our poor Lydia might be, we now long for certainty that it has occurred, since there is far too much cause to fear that they have not gone to Scotland. Colonel Forster arrived yesterday, having departed Brighton the previous day, only a few hours after the express. Lydia’s brief note to Mrs. F. had suggested that Gretna Green was their destination; but Denny let fall a remark declaring his belief that W. had never meant to go there, or indeed to marry Lydia. This was repeated to Colonel F., who became alarmed at once and left B. to follow their movements. He traced them readily enough to Clapham, but could proceed no farther. Upon arriving there, they exchanged the chaise that had brought them from Epsom for a hackney-coach and dismissed the former. Beyond this, all that is known is that someone saw them continue along the London road. I do not know what to believe. After pursuing every possible inquiry on that side of London, Colonel F. travelled into Hertfordshire, eagerly questioning people anew at every turnpike and at the inns in Barnet and Hatfield, but entirely without success: nobody had seen such travellers pass. With the utmost kindness and concern he continued to Longbourn and disclosed his fears in a fashion that did honour to his heart. I feel deeply for him and Mrs. F., though nobody can attach blame to either. Our anxiety, dear Lizzy, is extreme. My father and mother expect the worst, yet I cannot judge him so harshly. Many circumstances might make a private wedding in town preferable to their original scheme; and even if he were capable of such intentions toward a young woman with Lydia’s connections—which seems improbable—could I think her utterly lost to every consideration? It is impossible! I am distressed, however, to discover that Colonel F. is unwilling to rely upon their marriage. When I voiced my hopes, he shook his head and told me he feared W. was not trustworthy.
